t: Introduction: the topic and its relevance
n: In this lecture we consider the bioethical aspects of the problem of HIV and AIDS. The problem of HIV and AIDS touches almost all the ethical problems of modern medicine. Some ethical problems are characteristic of HIV infection alone. Many traditional principles of biomedicine are being tested precisely on the example of this infection. For example, the principle “Do no harm!” is under test: in many countries physicians refuse en masse to help people infected with HIV, the reason being personal safety. The plan of the session is as follows: the international response, concepts, testing of principles, the rights of people living with HIV, experimental treatment, and risk to medical workers.

t: The international response: the UN declaration and UNAIDS
n: First we look at the international response. The UN, that is, the United Nations General Assembly, adopted a political declaration on HIV on 2 June 2006. Prevention is regarded as the basis of the fight. It includes education in understandable language, reduction of risk behaviour, and supply of medicines. As the diagram shows, the international response consists of prevention, treatment, care and support, and also rights and gender equality. UNAIDS is the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV and AIDS, and protects rights and gender equality.

t: HIV and AIDS: distinguishing the concepts
n: Now we distinguish the concepts. HIV belongs to the group of retroviruses: its genetic material is not DNA but RNA. AIDS is singled out as an independent nosological unit, but in fact it is one of the stages of HIV infection. As the table shows, HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus, that is, the causative agent of the infection. AIDS, however, is the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, not the virus itself. Remember: HIV and AIDS are not the same thing. Do not confuse the virus with a stage of the disease; this is a place with a high risk of error.

t: Bioethical principles under the test of HIV
n: Many traditional principles and norms of bioethics are being tested precisely on the example of HIV infection. The problems of HIV and AIDS touch all the ethical questions of modern medicine, and some are characteristic of HIV infection alone. Once again we stress: HIV and AIDS are not the same concept. HIV is the human immunodeficiency virus, while AIDS is the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, one of the stages of HIV infection. Now we consider these principles in turn: “Do no harm!”, “Do good!”, then the principles of justice and human dignity.

t: The “Do no harm!” principle and refusal of help
n: We begin with the principle “Do no harm!”. Harm is not only physical: failing to help a patient is also a form of harm. In some countries physicians have refused en masse to help people infected with HIV. The reason for refusal is the personal safety of medical workers. Follow the chain in the diagram: a patient with HIV, the risk of infection to the physician, fear for personal safety, mass refusal of help, and as a result harm, that is, help is not given.

t: The internal contradiction in the “Do good!” principle
n: Now we consider the internal contradiction in the principle “Do good!”. The physician's beneficence is directed not only at the patient with HIV himself. It also covers questions of preventing HIV infection among the patient's close contacts. In an ordinary situation the physician preserves the health of one patient. In the case of HIV, however, those around must also be protected from infection. A worker who realises this experiences an internal contradiction and a split in professional thinking.

t: The principle of justice: legal and ethical aspects
n: Let us consider the legal and ethical aspects of the principle of justice. People living with HIV have equal rights under international law and national legislation. That is, in the legal, formal sense, they are equal to other citizens. However, ensuring equality for AIDS patients in practice is problematic. In the ethical, that is, substantive, sense, equality is hard to realise unconditionally. Therefore in the medical team there is a differentiated approach to such a patient. So the law says one thing, while practice is sometimes different.

t: The principle of autonomy in HIV/AIDS
n: We turn to the principle of autonomy. In HIV and AIDS the degree of the patient's autonomy is limited by external circumstances that affect the outcome of his actions. The main external circumstance is the patient's potential social danger; therefore ethical choice is determined by awareness of this danger. The patient's degree of freedom is limited by a high ethical and legal, even criminal, responsibility. At a certain stage of the disease, because of a grave physical and mental state, the patient may be incapable of autonomous action. Then the question of help in the agonal state, that is, the principle of human dignity, is also raised.

t: The principle of vulnerability and the UN declaration (2001)
n: Let us consider the principle of vulnerability and the UN declaration. There is a problem of implementing the principle of vulnerability with respect to patients with HIV and AIDS. The UN declaration of 27 June 2001 established that priority should be given to vulnerable groups. Expanding women's opportunities is considered very important for reducing vulnerability. Factors that increase vulnerability: poverty, lack of education and information, illiteracy, social alienation, discrimination and sexual exploitation.

t: Risk groups and differentiated attitudes
n: The question of risk groups and differentiated attitudes. The source classes as high-risk groups homosexual and bisexual persons, intravenous drug users, those engaged in prostitution, and donors. Because an improper way of life predominates among those infected, medical workers often call AIDS a punishment for improper behaviour. Specialists with such views begin to treat patients from different risk groups in a differentiated way, which often causes conflict. Remember: a risk group does not mean a patient who deserves punishment. Such differentiation is contrary to the principle of justice.

t: Case analysis 1: refusal of help
n: The first case analysis: refusal of help. The situation is this: a physician wants to refuse help to a patient with HIV because of personal safety. According to the source, failing to help is also a form of harm. In many countries physicians refused en masse because of personal safety. Under the principle “Do good” the physician's activity must also be directed to preserving the lives and health of others. This gives rise to an internal contradiction. Question: how does the reason of personal safety fit with the principles “Do no harm!” and justice? When is refusal justified?

t: Quick question 1
n: The first quick questions. Why do physicians refuse to help a person living with HIV? Because of personal safety; this is contrary to the principle “Do no harm”. Is the principle “Do good” directed only at the patient with HIV? No, it also covers protecting those around the patient from infection. What does justice demand? Legally, patients with HIV have equal rights, while in practice a differentiated attitude is met in the medical team. Remember also: HIV is an RNA retrovirus; AIDS is the acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, one of the stages of HIV infection.

t: A map of ethical questions
n: Now we look at the map of ethical questions. In the diagram there are four directions: informed consent, politicisation, stigmatisation and confidentiality. From the public health standpoint, prevention is carried out systematically across the whole state, through the media and education. The physician is a coach and confidant who respects the patient's right to make decisions. The risk of transmission to a partner is real, and if the patient does not tell, confidentiality may be breached; this is an extreme measure. The exception to confidentiality concerns precisely the partner who is at risk.

t: Informed consent and the human rights approach
n: Informed consent and the human rights approach. Blood sampling and treatment are carried out only with voluntary, informed consent. This principle is expressed in the Council of Europe document on human rights and biomedicine. The chain is as follows: information is given to the patient, voluntary consent is obtained, blood is taken for testing, and treatment is also carried out with consent. People living with HIV are full citizens who take part in developing strategy.

t: Public health and the politicisation of disease
n: On public health and the politicisation of disease. HIV prevention must cover the whole scale of the state. Systematic and comprehensive promotion must be carried out through the mass media, educational institutions, the workplace and advertising. The problem of HIV and AIDS is closely tied to questions of social order, for example social inequality. Thus in East Africa, in Kenya, the disease has penetrated all strata of society and families. The causes: poverty and women's lack of rights.

t: Stigmatisation
n: Let us speak of stigmatisation. A person with AIDS is seen by those around as a leper. This is stigmatisation, that is, a social stigma placed on the patient. Stigmatisation often results from healthcare workers breaching the rules of confidentiality. Remember: do not think that only society produces stigma. One cause is the breach of confidentiality by staff.

t: Fear, AIDS-phobia and directions of the fight
n: Fear, AIDS-phobia and directions of the fight. Fear rests on three factors: lack of information on HIV and AIDS, the inevitability of death, and society's negative attitude to patients. Shame, silence, discrimination and lack of confidentiality undermine prevention and care. The fight against AIDS is conducted in three directions: enlightenment, changing the negative social attitude, and deepening scientific research. Excessive fear can lead to AIDS-phobia, that is, fear of AIDS.

t: Physician and patient: coach and confidant
n: The physician–patient relationship: the role of coach and confidant. Many physicians may be under the influence of widespread unfounded stereotypes. Workers who have met new cases of AIDS must develop a sense of confidentiality towards patients and fight for the trust of risk groups. The physician must know that his patient is a future ally in the fight against a dangerous disease and must respect the patient's right to make decisions. Remember: in this situation the physician plays the role of coach and confidant and helps the patient to fight the disease.

t: Confidentiality and its exception
n: Confidentiality and its exception. A patient with AIDS, like other patients, has the right to secrecy; his sexual partner may thereby be at risk. The logic in the diagram is as follows: keeping the secret is the main rule. If the risk of transmission to the partner is evident, let the patient first inform the partner himself. If the patient refuses to inform, the physician may break the secrecy. Remember: disclosure of the secret is an exception and an extremely harsh measure, not the usual rule.

t: Individual rights and the safety of society
n: Individual rights and the safety of society. The epidemic of HIV and AIDS makes topical the problem of the relation between a person's individual rights and the interests of society's safety. Irresponsibility towards one's own health and deliberate violation of norms of conduct in dangerous situations violate the right of others to safety and health. All state structures that protect human rights and freedoms must pay particular attention to questions of HIV and AIDS. Remember: the relation between the individual right and the interests of society's safety is regarded as a separate problem.

t: Case analysis 2: notifying the partner
n: The second case analysis: notifying the partner. The situation: the sexual partner of a patient living with HIV is at real risk of infection, but the patient refuses to tell his partner. The physician seeks to protect the partner from harm, yet disclosure of information is a very serious measure. The concept of therapeutic collaboration is important here: in collaboration with the physician, the patient himself informs the partner. Question: what should the physician aim for before disclosure? What negative consequences might disclosure have?

t: Quick question 2
n: The second quick questions. How is blood taken for an HIV test? Only with voluntary, informed consent. Treatment is also carried out with the patient's consent. Why does stigmatisation arise? A patient with AIDS is treated like a leper; often the cause is staff breaching confidentiality. When may confidentiality be breached? If the risk of transmission is real and the patient refuses to tell his partner, the physician warns the partner. Remember: breaking confidentiality is a very heavy measure. First one must achieve that the patient himself informs the partner, that is, therapeutic collaboration.

t: Uzbek legislation: the main documents
n: Now we look at the main documents of Uzbek legislation. The basic document is the law on combating the spread of HIV, that is, human immunodeficiency virus, infection. According to the table, this law was adopted on 23 September 2013. The law incorporates the main international standards for protecting the rights of people infected with HIV and other vulnerable groups. Measures to combat it are carried out in accordance with the commitments of the Millennium and Dublin Declarations. The UN Millennium Declaration: 8 September 2000, resolution 55/2; the Dublin Declaration: 2004, for Europe and Central Asia.

t: Medical testing for HIV: three procedures
n: Let us look at the three procedures for medical testing for HIV. Testing is the study and assessment of a person's health. It establishes whether HIV is present. Counselling is provided before and after testing; for minors the consent of a legal representative is required. There are three procedures. Voluntary testing is at the person's wish, confidential and anonymous, at his own request. Mandatory testing is for categories listed in the law, for example donors and pregnant women. Compulsory testing is carried out without consent, by decision of an investigator or court ruling. Remember: mandatory and compulsory are not the same.

t: Stages of the testing process
n: Let us consider the stages of the testing process. In HIV testing, pre-test and post-test counselling is provided. The chain is as follows: pre-test counselling, laboratory testing, giving the result. If HIV is found, the person is warned in writing about criminal liability for infecting others. On request a certificate of absence of HIV is issued. It is issued at the AIDS centre, that is, the centre for acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, and is paid for.

t: Elements of an effective response
n: Let us consider the elements of an effective response. In the fight against HIV and AIDS, expanding access to a voluntary and confidential system of counselling and testing is of great importance. It is necessary to provide safe donor blood and early, effective treatment of sexually transmitted infections. Donor blood screening is carried out for certain indicators, including HIV-1 and HIV-2 antigens. In care, support and treatment, the highest standard is being developed on the basis of effective use of antiretroviral therapy. The diagram has five elements: counselling and testing, safe blood, treatment, care, and antiretroviral therapy.

t: Categories subject to mandatory testing
n: Categories subject to mandatory testing. Mandatory testing is undergone by donors of blood and biological fluids, persons marrying before the age of fifty, and pregnant women. Also tested are persons suspected of injecting drug use and children born to HIV-infected mothers. Workers who deal with blood, organs and tissues, and persons whose sexual partners have been found to have HIV, are also tested compulsorily. For some professions Article 15 applies. Remember: mandatory and compulsory are not the same. Compulsory testing is carried out without consent, only by decision of an inquiry officer or investigator or by court ruling.

t: Minors and persons lacking legal capacity
n: Testing of minors and persons lacking legal capacity. Minors and persons who lack legal capacity or have limited legal capacity are tested with the consent of their legal representatives. The result from the state laboratory is given not to such a person himself but to his legal representatives. If HIV is found, the staff of the medical institution inform the legal representatives and the institution where the person is. Compulsory testing is carried out without the consent of the person or his legal representative, on the basis of the decision of an inquiry officer or investigator or a court ruling.

t: The legal rights of people living with HIV
n: The legal rights of people living with HIV. The law lays down the rights of persons infected with HIV and those at risk of infection. The diagram shows four groups: testing and counselling, document, confidentiality, help and information. A person can be tested and receive counselling, and a written answer, that is, a certificate, is issued for the result. The secret is kept, and anonymous testing is also possible. The person is also informed of liability for infecting others with HIV. The right to free medical help and treatment in connection with HIV is also granted.

t: Social support for children
n: Social support for children. Persons infected with HIV under 18, irrespective of the stage of disease, receive a monthly social allowance and the benefits of disabled children. Parents or guardians are temporarily released from work and have the right to stay with the child in hospital with receipt of an allowance. If HIV is found in a minor, medical workers inform his legal representatives. Remember: for the right to the allowance the stage of the disease, that is, HIV or AIDS, does not matter.

t: Cases where discrimination is not permitted
n: Cases where discrimination is not permitted. The law does not permit four kinds of discrimination against people living with HIV. First, dismissal from work or refusal of employment. Second, refusal of admission to an educational institution. Third, refusal of admission to a medical institution. Fourth, restriction of the right to housing and other rights. The right to housing is retained both for the person infected with HIV and for his family members. Remember: the prohibition is not absolute. The exceptions are certain professions on the ministry's list and certain types of education set by law.

t: Restrictions: donation and the list of professions
n: Restrictions: donation and the list of professions. Persons infected with the human immunodeficiency virus, that is, HIV, cannot be donors of blood and biological fluids. The list of the Ministry of Justice of 7 May 2014 prohibits persons infected with HIV from 9 types of professional activity. The head of an organisation who permits work on the list is held responsible. The table gives the work removed from the old list: provision of medical care, production of vaccines and pharmaceutical products, massage procedures, and contact sports.

t: Case analysis 3: hiring and professional restriction
n: The third case analysis: hiring and professional restriction. The situation: an employee living with HIV is working at his former organisation. His work is not on the list of prohibited professions, but the manager wants to dismiss him. The law prohibits termination of the employment contract of people living with HIV and refusal to hire them. Certain professions are an exception. Remember: having HIV does not mean that a person cannot work in any job. The prohibition applies only to the types of activity on the list. Question: does the manager's decision accord with the law? What liability does a manager bear who has admitted a worker to a profession on the list?

t: The Law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health”
n: Let us look at the law “On the Protection of Citizens' Health”. Citizens receive timely, accurate information about factors affecting health, the sanitary state of the area, norms of nutrition and the safety of services. In illness or loss of working capacity there is a right to medical and social help: treatment, rehabilitation, sanatorium, prosthesis and a temporary allowance. Information about a consultation, state of health, diagnosis and data obtained during examination and treatment is kept secret. This right to medical confidentiality is laid down in law. If harm to health is caused in providing medical care, the harm is compensated in the manner established by law. A person living with HIV, as a patient, also has these rights.

t: Experimental treatment: trials without a placebo
n: Experimental treatment and trials without a placebo. In some countries drugs for the human immunodeficiency virus, that is, HIV, may be tested without a placebo. Help for an AIDS patient, that is, a patient with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, in the agonal state is regarded as an ethical problem. In severe cases the question of realising the principle of human dignity becomes acute. The chain is as follows: a severe stage of the disease, a grave physical and mental state, sharpening of the question of dignity, and the problem of help in the agonal state.

t: Medical advances, drug prices and truthfulness
n: Medical advances, drug prices and truthfulness. AIDS patients know the negative outcome of the disease is inevitable, and are therefore sensitive to any information about a new drug. Treatment with an “HIV protease inhibitor” costs at least 20 000 dollars a year; not every patient can buy it, and this raises the problem of communication. New diagnostic test systems detect HIV antibodies in 1 to 5 minutes; four vaccines are undergoing first-stage clinical trials. More than 50 new highly active chemotherapy drugs against HIV are in clinical trials.

t: The principle of integrity and new medical technologies
n: The principle of integrity and new medical technologies. HIV and AIDS remain a little-studied area of medicine. The number of studies markedly exceeds the number of positive practical results achieved. Follow the path in the diagram: a little-studied area, many studies and few results, a new technology is created, and in clinical use the risk grows. That is, a new technology in the clinic may increase the threat to the physical and mental integrity of the person.

t: Case analysis 4: experimental treatment
n: The fourth case analysis: experimental treatment. The situation: a patient living with HIV has been offered treatment with a new drug created in a little-studied area. According to the source, treatment too must be carried out with the patient's voluntary, informed consent. A new technology may increase the threat to the physical and mental integrity of the person. Question: what risks must the physician explain to the patient when obtaining consent, and why?

t: Occupational risks of medical workers
n: Occupational risks of medical workers. In many countries physicians refuse en masse to help people with HIV. The reason for refusal is the worker's personal safety, and the ethical assessment is that failing to help is also harm. Workers who deal with blood, biological fluids, organs and tissues are tested for HIV compulsorily, as laid down in Article 15. A worker who has failed to perform, or has performed poorly, a professional duty is obliged to compensate the harm caused.

t: Conclusion: key takeaways and a quick question
n: Let us conclude. The 2013 law guarantees people living with HIV, that is, the human immunodeficiency virus, free help, a certificate and the right to work, with exceptions. On confidentiality and consent: testing is voluntary, with counselling, and confidential. The partner may be informed only in real danger and where the patient refuses. On experimental treatment and occupational risk: a new technology may threaten the integrity of the person; workers, for their part, refuse because of personal risk. Quick question: why can refusing help also violate the principle “Do no harm!”?
